# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall campaign.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall campaign)
B1. Background checks: series figure is "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" (Cook & Ludwig, National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms).
B2. Children: use the ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children"; child gun deaths are "children shot and killed".
B3. Headline toll: 46,728 "killed by gun violence". The fall campaign does not break deaths out by intent.
B4. Mass shootings: GVA's 656 for 2023, as "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston".
B5. Assault weapons: series line is "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings".
B6. Source line for B1-B5 figures: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research". Appendix notes: source line only.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B6 for B1-B5; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, DC
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1-17 for the fourth straight year.
- Federal law screens only part of the gun market: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Military-style rifles turn up in under 3 percent of U.S. murders overall, but when they appear in public attacks, roughly twice as many people are killed.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help states adopt extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, according to final federal mortality data. That is one death every 11 minutes. Only two years on record, 2021 and 2022, were deadlier, and the gun death rate fell about 3 percent from 2022 to 2023.

That decline deserves to be stated plainly, because it was earned by communities, hospitals and local violence-interruption programs that have worked to bend these numbers down. It is also nowhere near enough. Every one of those deaths left a family planning a funeral, a classroom with an empty desk, a workplace with a missing colleague. A brief that opens with a number should be honest about what the number is: the compiled record of a year of private grief, assembled one 911 call at a time.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll falls hardest in ways that should command Congress's attention. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1-17 died from gun violence, a rate of 3.7 per 100,000. That is seven young people shot and killed every day. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death for this age group, killing more children and teens than car crashes, cancer or drug overdoses.

The measure matters when members talk about this at home. Sixty-three percent of these deaths were homicides; 29 percent were suicides, a reminder that the gun suicide crisis reaches into childhood. A broader published measure that counts 18- and 19-year-olds and pools the years 2021 through 2023 puts the rate at 5.9 per 100,000. No reading of the data, however constructed, returns a picture of a country keeping its children safe.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect, every purchase from a licensed gun dealer must clear a background check run through the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System. That is the floor of federal law, and the floor has a hole in it. In most states, a private seller is not required to run any check at all, so sales arranged at gun shows, through online classifieds or between strangers in parking lots can legally bypass the screen that applies to a purchase from a dealer. Federally prohibited purchasers know where to shop.

The best recent national measure of how big the gap is comes from a 2015 survey published in Annals of Internal Medicine: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a gun in the previous two years reported doing so without a background check. An older and widely cited figure, that 40 percent of sales evade checks, traces to a 1994 survey that measured acquisitions generally, including gifts and inheritances, and did not ask about checks; the authors' own sales-only reanalysis put the sales figure at 14 to 22 percent. We cite the 22 percent estimate because it is direct, recent and peer reviewed, and it still means that roughly one in five recent gun acquisitions cleared no check at all.

The policy is popular in a way almost nothing else in Washington is: 92 percent of registered voters, polled by Quinnipiac in November 2023, support requiring background checks for all gun buyers, including majorities of gun owners. The research record shows that dealer background checks are associated with reduced firearm homicide, and states that have extended checks to private sales have seen reductions in overall homicide. This is not a leap of faith. It is closing a hole that the rest of the law already condemns.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, defined as incidents in which four or more people were shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter. That is nearly two a day, leaving 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. The named attacks Americans remember most, Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023, were all carried out with AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles.

The honest argument for an assault weapons ban is not that these rifles dominate U.S. murders. They do not; rifles of every type, which the FBI does not break out by style, were the weapon in under 3 percent of murders in 2018. The argument is what these weapons do in the moments they are used. Analysis of 248 active shooter incidents from 2000 through 2017 found that when a semiautomatic rifle was present, the attack killed an average of 4.25 people and wounded 5.48, against averages of 2.49 killed and 3.02 wounded for attacks without one. Nearly twice the wounded, nearly twice the dead, in the attacks that dominate the news and shape how Americans feel about public life.

The United States has tested this policy. The 1994 federal assault weapons ban barred the manufacture and sale of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and it grandfathered existing stock rather than confiscating it. It expired on September 13, 2004, and it never got a full decade of clean data, because grandfathered guns kept the banned features in circulation. Federal assessments found the use of banned guns in crime declined in the cities studied, while concluding the ban's effect on overall violence was uncertain; newer research finds that restrictions on large-capacity magazines are associated with fewer deaths in high-fatality mass shootings. A modern ban should apply to future manufacture and sale, and this time pair it with a buyback that shrinks the grandfathered stock.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require an NICS check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales arranged at gun shows and online, so that the standard a licensed dealer must meet applies to every sale.
2. **Reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's prohibition on the manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, fund a voluntary buyback to reduce the grandfathered stock, and write definitions by function so the industry cannot engineer around them.
3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research at a scale commensurate with a toll of 46,728 deaths, and codify that federal research on the causes and prevention of gun violence is authorized public health work.
4. **Help states adopt extreme-risk laws.** Create a competitive grant program for states that enact extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily separate firearms from people who pose a documented danger to themselves or others, and condition funds on strong due-process protections. Indiana's decade of experience with a risk-based seizure law is associated with a 7.5 percent drop in firearm suicides.

## Closing the gaps

None of these numbers describes an act of nature. They describe the predictable results of laws that stop halfway: checks that apply to some sellers and not others, and a rifle ban that was allowed to expire with its stock grandfathered in place. Congress wrote those gaps into law, and Congress can write them out. The families behind this year's figures should not have to accept them."}

{"content": "# Data appendix — Safer Communities Brief No. 9

"Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban"
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention, Northgate Progress Institute
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

**Production note on source lines.** Style sheet C1 requires source lines in the form Agency/author, Title, Date, except that B1-B5 campaign figures carry the series line "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research." That series line is reproduced below where it applies, alongside the full citation, because two of the campaign figures (Gun Violence Archive, America's Health Rankings) are not federal datasets and the series line alone would misattribute them. Full citations are used throughout so Hill offices and reporters can trace every number. Editorial sign-off required.

**Production note on intent data.** Per style sheet B3, the fall campaign presents the headline toll (46,728) without an intent breakdown, and all persuasive copy in this package follows that. Composition rows from the underlying analysis are included in Table 1 for auditability and can be cut.

## Table 1. U.S. gun deaths, 2023

| Indicator | 2023 |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths | 46,728 |
| Equivalent frequency | one death every 11 minutes |
| Rank among all years on record | third-highest annual total |
| Change in overall gun death rate from 2022 | down about 3 percent |
| Composition (for reference; see B3 note) | suicides 27,300 (58%); homicides 17,927 |
| Homicide trend | 17,927 in 2023, down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022 |

Source: CDC, WONDER Compressed Mortality, 2023 final data; analysis in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025. Series source line per style sheet B6: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research."

Note: The total spans all intents. JHU reports that gun suicides were 58 percent of the 2023 total, a record high, and that gun homicides declined for a second straight year. One death every 11 minutes is 525,600 minutes divided by 46,728 deaths.

## Table 2. Children and teens ages 1-17, 2023

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| Deaths | 2,566 |
| Rate | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Deaths per day | about 7 |
| Leading cause of death | firearms, 4th consecutive year, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses |
| Intent: homicide | 63% |
| Intent: suicide | 29% |
| Intent: unintentional | 5% |
| Intent: undetermined or other | 3% |

Source: CDC WONDER, 2023 final data, tabulated in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025.

Note: JHU reports the ages 1-17 death rate rose about 2 percent from 2022. House phrasing per style sheet B2: deaths of children and teens are described as "children shot and killed."

## Table 3. Youth firearm death rate, ages 1-19

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Rate, ages 1-19, pooled 2021-2023 | 5.9 per 100,000 |

Source: America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Firearm deaths among children ages 1-19," pooled 2021-2023, from CDC WONDER.

Note for editors: this is the series rate carried in style sheet B2. It is not a single-year children's rate: it includes 18- and 19-year-olds, who are legal adults with markedly higher gun death rates, and it pools three years, including the 2021 record year. The 2023 single-year rate for ages 1-17 is 3.7 per 100,000 (Table 2). Brief No. 9 uses the ages 1-17 figure and cites this measure only with its full label. Sign-off required if the campaign wants it used unlabeled.

## Table 4. Firearm acquisitions without a background check

| Estimate | Figure | What was measured |
|---|---|---|
| 2015 national survey | 22% | of gun owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years, those who acquired it without a background check |
| 1994 NSPOF, original estimate | about 40% | of recently acquired guns came from a source other than a licensed dealer, including gifts and inheritances |
| 1994 NSPOF, sales-only reanalysis | 14-22% | share of sales, not acquisitions, without a background check |

Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, "Firearm acquisition without background checks: results of a national survey," Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017 (2015 survey, n=1,613 gun owners); Cook and Ludwig, "Guns in America: National Survey on Private Ownership and Use of Firearms," National Institute of Justice, 1997 (1994 NSPOF survey). Series source line per style sheet B6: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research."

Note for editors: the 1994 NSPOF did not ask about background checks and predates full implementation of the Brady Act; the "40 percent of gun sales" formulation has been rated Mostly False (PolitiFact, February 2018) and called stale (Washington Post Fact Checker, January 2013). Brief No. 9 therefore leads with the direct 2015 figure (22 percent) and does not use the B1 series line as written. Sign-off required.

## Table 5. Public support for background checks on all gun buyers

| Poll | Population | Support |
|---|---|---|
| Quinnipiac University national poll, November 2023 | registered voters | 92% |

Source: Quinnipiac University Polling Institute, national survey of registered voters, November 2, 2023.

Note: separate national surveying of gun owners (97Percent, December 2024, n=5,100 gun owners who are registered voters) finds about 85 percent support universal background checks.

## Table 6. Research evidence on background-check laws

| Policy | Evidence finding |
|---|---|
| Dealer background checks | moderate evidence of a reduction in firearm homicide |
| Universal background checks (dealer plus private sales) | moderate evidence of a reduction in total homicide; limited evidence on firearm homicide |
| Universal background checks and suicide | inconclusive |

Source: RAND, Gun Policy in America, "The Effects of Background Checks" evidence review (accessed October 2026); RAND, "The Science of Gun Policy," fifth edition, 2023.

Note: RAND grades studies it considers methodologically adequate; "inconclusive" means the available studies do not yet support a conclusion, not that evidence of no effect was found.

## Table 7. Mass shootings, 2023

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings (Gun Violence Archive) | 656 |
| People killed in those incidents | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |
| Frequency | nearly two per day |
| Mass killings, AP/USA Today/Northeastern database | 36 incidents as of late October 2023 (4 or more killed; partial year) |

Source: Gun Violence Archive, "Mass Shootings" report, 2023; killed and injured counts as compiled by Axios, January 9, 2024; AP/USA Today/Northeastern University mass-killing database, October 2023.

Note: GVA defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter; the AP/USA Today/Northeastern database counts four or more killed. The two counts answer different questions and are not comparable. GVA is a private nonprofit data project, not a federal dataset; the series source line "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research" does not cover this table. Per style sheet B4 the series framing is "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston"; those attacks (2022, 2018, 2023) were carried out with AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles.

## Table 8. Rifles in U.S. murders (all rifle types)

| Year | Share of murders | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 2.6% | not separately published in source table |
| 2018 | 2.8% | 297 murders |

Source: FBI, Uniform Crime Reports Expanded Homicide Data, 2017 and 2018.

Note: the FBI does not separate AR-style rifles from other rifles. The brief's assault weapons argument rests on lethality in public mass shootings (Table 9), not on rifles' overall share of murders, which is under 3 percent.

## Table 9. Lethality of active shooter incidents with and without semiautomatic rifles

| Measure | With semiautomatic rifle | Without |
|---|---|---|
| Share of incidents, 2000-2017 | 24.6% (61 of 248) | 75.4% (187) |
| Mean persons wounded | 5.48 | 3.02 |
| Mean persons killed | 4.25 | 2.49 |
| Mean persons wounded or killed | 9.72 | 5.47 |
| Incidence rate ratio, wounded | 1.81 (95% CI, 1.30-2.53) | |
| Incidence rate ratio, killed | 1.97 (95% CI, 1.38-2.80) | |

Source: de Jager, Goralnick, McCarty, Hashmi, Jarman and Haider, "Lethality of civilian active shooter incidents with and without semiautomatic rifles in the United States," JAMA, 2018.

Note: the share of wounded people who died was similar in both groups (about 44 percent with a semiautomatic rifle present); the difference in deaths is driven by more people being shot, not by deadlier wounds. Handguns remain the most common firearm in mass shootings (used in about 80 percent of attacks per The Violence Project database), so the series line "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings" (style sheet B5) is not supported as written. The defensible series line is that assault weapons are the weapon of choice in the deadliest mass shootings. Sign-off required.

## Table 10. Federal assault weapons ban, 1994-2004

| Provision or finding | Detail |
|---|---|
| Enacted | September 1994 |
| Prohibited | manufacture and sale of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines (more than 10 rounds) |
| Existing stock | grandfathered; no confiscation |
| Expiration | September 13, 2004 |
| NIJ assessment of banned-gun use in crime | declined 17% to 72% across the localities studied (1995-2003 post-ban period) |
| NIJ assessment of overall crime effect | uncertain; grandfathered stock limited measurable effect |
| RAND evidence grade for bans' effect on violent crime and mass shootings | inconclusive |
| Large-capacity magazine bans and high-fatality mass shootings | associated with fewer deaths |

Source: Koper, "Updated Assessment of the Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Impacts on Gun Markets and Gun Violence, 1994-2003," National Institute of Justice, 2004; RAND, "The Science of Gun Policy," fifth edition, 2023; Klarevas, McCartney and Vernick, "Assessing the potential to reduce deaths and injuries from mass shootings through restrictions on assault weapons and other high-capacity semiautomatic firearms," Criminology and Public Policy, 2019.

Note: the same research review finds high-capacity semiautomatics (assault weapons as a subset) used in 20 to 58 percent of firearm mass murders, and in a particularly high share of public mass shootings. Recommendation 2's buyback proposal is designed to address the grandfathering constraint NIJ identified.

## Table 11. Extreme-risk (red flag) laws: suicide outcomes

| State | Finding |
|---|---|
| Indiana | risk-based firearm seizure law (2006) associated with a 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides over 10 years |
| Connecticut | law (1999) associated with a 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides in the post-Virginia Tech enforcement period |

Source: Kivisto and Phalen, "Effects of risk-based firearm seizure laws in Connecticut and Indiana on suicide rates, 1981-2015," Psychiatric Services, 2018.

Note: RAND grades the broader ERPO literature as inconclusive for suicide overall; the Connecticut and Indiana studies are the strongest quasi-experimental evidence and used synthetic controls. Recommendation 4 includes due-process conditions in part to answer the objections raised in this literature.

## Definitions

- **Assault weapons:** semiautomatic firearms with detachable magazines and the military-style features defined in the 1994 federal ban (style sheet A2). The outline's category is the one used in Table 10.
- **Mass shooting:** four or more people shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter (Gun Violence Archive).
- **Universal background checks:** extension of the licensed-dealer NICS requirement to all firearm sales and transfers.

## Series figures used from the fall campaign (style sheet B1-B5), with handling

| Series figure | Handling in this package |
|---|---|
| B1: "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" | not used as written; replaced with 22% (2015 survey) and the 14-22% sales reanalysis; provenance in Table 4 |
| B2: ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children" | used only with its full label; brief leads with ages 1-17 (3.7 per 100,000); see Table 3 note |
| B3: 46,728 "killed by gun violence," no intent breakdown | used in all persuasive copy per B3; composition rows retained in appendix Table 1 |
| B4: 656 mass shootings (GVA), "like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston" | used; definitional note in Table 7 |
| B5: "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings" | not used as written; replaced with the lethality finding (Table 9) and "deadliest mass shootings" framing; see Table 9 note |", "path": "/workspace/out/data_appendix.md"}

{"content": "# Fact sheet: Closing the gaps on gun violence

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026
For use by congressional offices. Full citations and notes: data appendix to Brief No. 9.

## Eight numbers for the record

**1. 46,728** Americans killed by gun violence in 2023. One every 11 minutes; the third-highest annual total on record, down about 3 percent from 2022.
Source: CDC WONDER 2023 final data, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**2. 2,566** children and teens ages 1-17 killed by gun violence in 2023: 3.7 per 100,000, about seven young people every day.
Source: CDC WONDER 2023 final data, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**3. Fourth straight year** firearms were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1-17, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses.
Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, analysis of CDC WONDER 2023 data, June 2025.

**4. 22 percent** of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years acquired it without a background check (2015 national survey of 1,613 owners).
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**5. 92 percent** of registered voters support requiring background checks for all gun buyers.
Source: Quinnipiac University national poll, November 2023.

**6. 656** mass shootings in 2023, four or more people shot per incident, excluding the shooter: 712 killed and 2,692 injured.
Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023; casualty compilation by Axios, January 2024.

**7. About twice as many killed and wounded** in active shooter attacks when a semiautomatic rifle is present (mean 4.25 killed and 5.48 wounded per incident, versus 2.49 and 3.02 without).
Source: de Jager et al., JAMA, 2018.

**8. 7.5 percent fewer** firearm suicides in Indiana over a decade following its risk-based firearm seizure law.
Source: Kivisto and Phalen, Psychiatric Services, 2018.

## What Brief No. 9 asks Congress to do

1. Pass universal background checks, covering private sales at gun shows and online.
2. Reinstate the assault weapons ban, bar large-capacity magazines, and fund a voluntary buyback of grandfathered stock.
3. Fund firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and NIH at a scale commensurate with a toll of 46,728 deaths.
4. Create a matching grant program, with due-process conditions, for states that enact extreme-risk protection orders.

Media contact: Northgate Progress Institute Office of Communications, Washington, DC.", "path": "/workspace/out/fact_sheet.md"}

WASHINGTON (October 27, 2026) — Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and firearms remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17 for the fourth straight year, according to a brief released today by the Northgate Progress Institute.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Senior Fellow Dr. Jamal Whitfield, argues that two gaps in federal law cost lives: a background-check requirement that exempts private sales, and the 2004 expiration of the assault weapons ban.

The brief finds that 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years acquired it without a background check, while 92 percent of registered voters support checks on all gun buyers. It documents 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured, and finds that attacks carried out with semiautomatic rifles kill and wound about twice as many people as other active shooter attacks.

"Every figure in this brief is a family's grief," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at NPI. "The gaps that let guns reach dangerous hands, and put battlefield rifles on our main streets, were written into federal law. They were choices, and Congress can make different ones."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks covering private sales; reinstate the assault weapons ban with new restrictions on large-capacity magazines and a voluntary buyback of grandfathered stock; fund firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and NIH; and help states enact extreme-risk laws with due-process protections.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, DC
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1-17 for the fourth straight year.
- Federal law screens only part of the gun market: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Military-style rifles turn up in under 3 percent of U.S. murders overall, but when they appear in public attacks, roughly twice as many people are killed.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help states adopt extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, according to final federal mortality data. That is one death every 11 minutes. Only two years on record, 2021 and 2022, were deadlier, and the gun death rate fell about 3 percent from 2022 to 2023.

That decline deserves to be stated plainly, because it was earned by communities, hospitals and local violence-interruption programs that have worked to bend these numbers down. It is also nowhere near enough. Every one of those deaths left a family planning a funeral, a classroom with an empty desk, a workplace with a missing colleague. A brief that opens with a number should be honest about what the number is: the compiled record of a year of private grief, assembled one 911 call at a time.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll falls hardest in ways that should command Congress's attention. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1-17 died from gun violence, a rate of 3.7 per 100,000. That is seven young people shot and killed every day. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death for this age group, killing more children and teens than car crashes, cancer or drug overdoses.

The measure matters when members talk about this at home. Sixty-three percent of these deaths were homicides; 29 percent were suicides, a reminder that the gun suicide crisis reaches into childhood. A broader published measure that counts 18- and 19-year-olds and pools the years 2021 through 2023 puts the rate at 5.9 per 100,000. No reading of the data, however constructed, returns a picture of a country keeping its children safe.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect, every purchase from a licensed gun dealer must clear a background check run through the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System. That is the floor of federal law, and the floor has a hole in it. In most states, a private seller is not required to run any check at all, so sales arranged at gun shows, through online classifieds or between strangers in parking lots can legally bypass the screen that applies to a purchase from a dealer. Federally prohibited purchasers know where to shop.

The best recent national measure of how big the gap is comes from a 2015 survey published in Annals of Internal Medicine: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a gun in the previous two years reported doing so without a background check. An older and widely cited figure, that 40 percent of sales evade checks, traces to a 1994 survey that measured acquisitions generally, including gifts and inheritances, and did not ask about checks; the authors' own sales-only reanalysis put the sales figure at 14 to 22 percent. We cite the 22 percent estimate because it is direct, recent and peer reviewed, and it still means that roughly one in five recent gun acquisitions cleared no check at all.

The policy is popular in a way almost nothing else in Washington is: 92 percent of registered voters, polled by Quinnipiac in November 2023, support requiring background checks for all gun buyers, including majorities of gun owners. The research record shows that dealer background checks are associated with reduced firearm homicide, and states that have extended checks to private sales have seen reductions in overall homicide. This is not a leap of faith. It is closing a hole that the rest of the law already condemns.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, defined as incidents in which four or more people were shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter. That is nearly two a day, leaving 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. The named attacks Americans remember most, Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023, were all carried out with AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles.

The honest argument for an assault weapons ban is not that these rifles dominate U.S. murders. They do not; rifles of every type, which the FBI does not break out by style, were the weapon in under 3 percent of murders in 2018. The argument is what these weapons do in the moments they are used. Analysis of 248 active shooter incidents from 2000 through 2017 found that when a semiautomatic rifle was present, the attack killed an average of 4.25 people and wounded 5.48, against averages of 2.49 killed and 3.02 wounded for attacks without one. Nearly twice the wounded, nearly twice the dead, in the attacks that dominate the news and shape how Americans feel about public life.

The United States has tested this policy. The 1994 federal assault weapons ban barred the manufacture and sale of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and it grandfathered existing stock rather than confiscating it. It expired on September 13, 2004, and it never got a full decade of clean data, because grandfathered guns kept the banned features in circulation. Federal assessments found the use of banned guns in crime declined in the cities studied, while concluding the ban's effect on overall violence was uncertain; newer research finds that restrictions on large-capacity magazines are associated with fewer deaths in high-fatality mass shootings. A modern ban should apply to future manufacture and sale, and this time pair it with a buyback that shrinks the grandfathered stock.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require an NICS check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales arranged at gun shows and online, so that the standard a licensed dealer must meet applies to every sale.
2. **Reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's prohibition on the manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, fund a voluntary buyback to reduce the grandfathered stock, and write definitions by function so the industry cannot engineer around them.
3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research at a scale commensurate with a toll of 46,728 deaths, and codify that federal research on the causes and prevention of gun violence is authorized public health work.
4. **Help states adopt extreme-risk laws.** Create a competitive grant program for states that enact extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily separate firearms from people who pose a documented danger to themselves or others, and condition funds on strong due-process protections. Indiana's decade of experience with a risk-based seizure law is associated with a 7.5 percent drop in firearm suicides.

## Closing the gaps

None of these numbers describes an act of nature. They describe the predictable results of laws that stop halfway: checks that apply to some sellers and not others, and a rifle ban that was allowed to expire with its stock grandfathered in place. Congress wrote those gaps into law, and Congress can write them out. The families behind this year's figures should not have to accept them.
Two precision fixes needed: the exec-summary rifle share (all rifles are under 3 percent of murders; the military-style subset is unknown) and the AWB expiry sentence.

Media contact: [NPI communications office to confirm name, phone and email]

## Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban would save lives, NPI brief finds

WASHINGTON, October 27, 2026. Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and firearms remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17 for the fourth straight year, according to a brief released today by the Northgate Progress Institute.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Senior Fellow Dr. Jamal Whitfield, argues that two gaps in federal law cost lives: a background-check requirement that exempts private sales, and the 2004 expiration of the assault weapons ban.

The brief finds 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years got no background check, while 92 percent of registered voters support checks on all gun buyers. It documents 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 dead and 2,692 injured, and finds attacks with semiautomatic rifles kill and wound about twice as many people.

"Every figure in this brief is a family's grief," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at NPI. "The gaps that let guns reach dangerous hands, and put battlefield rifles on our main streets, were written into federal law. They were choices, and Congress can make different ones."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks covering private sales; reinstate the assault weapons ban with new restrictions on large-capacity magazines and a voluntary buyback of grandfathered stock; fund firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and NIH; and help states enact extreme-risk laws with due-process protections.

The brief, fact sheet and data appendix are available from the institute. The Northgate Progress Institute is a Washington, DC think tank working to expand economic security, protect public health and make communities safer.

# Data appendix: Safer Communities Brief No. 9

"Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban"
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention, Northgate Progress Institute
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

**Production note on source lines.** Style sheet C1 requires source lines in the form Agency/author, Title, Date, except that B1-B5 campaign figures carry the series line "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research." That series line is reproduced below where it applies, alongside the full citation, because two of the campaign figures (Gun Violence Archive, America's Health Rankings) are not federal datasets and the series line alone would misattribute them. Full citations are used throughout so Hill offices and reporters can trace every number. Editorial sign-off required.

**Production note on intent data.** Per style sheet B3, the fall campaign presents the headline toll (46,728) without an intent breakdown, and all persuasive copy in this package follows that. Composition rows from the underlying analysis are included in Table 1 for auditability and can be cut.

## Table 1. U.S. gun deaths, 2023

| Indicator | 2023 |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths | 46,728 |
| Equivalent frequency | one death every 11 minutes |
| Rank among all years on record | third-highest annual total |
| Change in overall gun death rate from 2022 | down about 3 percent |
| Composition (for reference; see B3 note) | suicides 27,300 (58%); homicides 17,927 |
| Homicide trend | 17,927 in 2023, down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022 |

Source: CDC, WONDER Compressed Mortality, 2023 final data; analysis in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025. Series source line per style sheet B6: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research."

Note: The total spans all intents. JHU reports that gun suicides were 58 percent of the 2023 total, a record high, and that gun homicides declined for a second straight year. One death every 11 minutes is 525,600 minutes divided by 46,728 deaths.

## Table 2. Children and teens ages 1-17, 2023

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| Deaths | 2,566 |
| Rate | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Deaths per day | about 7 |
| Leading cause of death | firearms, 4th consecutive year, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses |
| Intent: homicide | 63% |
| Intent: suicide | 29% |
| Intent: unintentional | 5% |
| Intent: undetermined or other | 3% |

Source: CDC WONDER, 2023 final data, tabulated in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025.

Note: JHU reports the ages 1-17 death rate rose about 2 percent from 2022. House phrasing per style sheet B2: deaths of children and teens are described as "children shot and killed."

## Table 3. Youth firearm death rate, ages 1-19

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Rate, ages 1-19, pooled 2021-2023 | 5.9 per 100,000 |

Source: America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Firearm deaths among children ages 1-19," pooled 2021-2023, from CDC WONDER.

Note for editors: this is the series rate carried in style sheet B2. It is not a single-year children's rate: it includes 18- and 19-year-olds, who are legal adults with markedly higher gun death rates, and it pools three years, including the 2021 record year. The 2023 single-year rate for ages 1-17 is 3.7 per 100,000 (Table 2). Brief No. 9 uses the ages 1-17 figure and cites this measure only with its full label. # Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9**
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention
Northgate Progress Institute, Washington, DC
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one death every 11 minutes, and firearms remain the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1-17 for the fourth straight year.
- Federal law screens only part of the gun market: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Rifles of all types, military-style included, are used in under 3 percent of U.S. murders, but when military-style rifles appear in public attacks, roughly twice as many people are killed.
- Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban, fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH, and help states adopt extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, according to final federal mortality data. That is one death every 11 minutes. Only two years on record, 2021 and 2022, were deadlier, and the gun death rate fell about 3 percent from 2022 to 2023.

That decline deserves to be stated plainly, because it was earned by communities, hospitals and local violence-interruption programs that have worked to bend these numbers down. It is also nowhere near enough. Every one of those deaths left a family planning a funeral, a classroom with an empty desk, a workplace with a missing colleague. A brief that opens with a number should be honest about what the number is: the compiled record of a year of private grief, assembled one 911 call at a time.

## 2. Children and teens

The toll falls hardest in ways that should command Congress's attention. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens ages 1-17 died from gun violence, a rate of 3.7 per 100,000. That is seven young people shot and killed every day. For the fourth consecutive year, firearms were the leading cause of death for this age group, killing more children and teens than car crashes, cancer or drug overdoses.

The measure matters when members talk about this at home. Sixty-three percent of these deaths were homicides; 29 percent were suicides, a reminder that the gun suicide crisis reaches into childhood. A broader published measure that counts 18- and 19-year-olds and pools the years 2021 through 2023 puts the rate at 5.9 per 100,000. No reading of the data, however constructed, returns a picture of a country keeping its children safe.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since the Brady Act took effect, every purchase from a licensed gun dealer must clear a background check run through the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System. That is the floor of federal law, and the floor has a hole in it. In most states, a private seller is not required to run any check at all, so sales arranged at gun shows, through online classifieds or between strangers in parking lots can legally bypass the screen that applies to a purchase from a dealer. Federally prohibited purchasers know where to shop.

The best recent national measure of how big the gap is comes from a 2015 survey published in Annals of Internal Medicine: 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a gun in the previous two years reported doing so without a background check. An older and widely cited figure, that 40 percent of sales evade checks, traces to a 1994 survey that measured acquisitions generally, including gifts and inheritances, and did not ask about checks; the authors' own sales-only reanalysis put the sales figure at 14 to 22 percent. We cite the 22 percent estimate because it is direct, recent and peer reviewed, and it still means that roughly one in five recent gun acquisitions cleared no check at all.

The policy is popular in a way almost nothing else in Washington is: 92 percent of registered voters, polled by Quinnipiac in November 2023, support requiring background checks for all gun buyers, including majorities of gun owners. The research record shows that dealer background checks are associated with reduced firearm homicide, and states that have extended checks to private sales have seen reductions in overall homicide. This is not a leap of faith. It is closing a hole that the rest of the law already condemns.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, defined as incidents in which four or more people were shot, killed or injured, not counting the shooter. That is nearly two a day, leaving 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. The named attacks Americans remember most, Uvalde in 2022, Parkland in 2018 and Lewiston in 2023, were all carried out with AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles.

The honest argument for an assault weapons ban is not that these rifles dominate U.S. murders. They do not; rifles of every type, which the FBI does not break out by style, were the weapon in under 3 percent of murders in 2018. The argument is what these weapons do in the moments they are used. Analysis of 248 active shooter incidents from 2000 through 2017 found that when a semiautomatic rifle was present, the attack killed an average of 4.25 people and wounded 5.48, against averages of 2.49 killed and 3.02 wounded for attacks without one. Nearly twice the wounded, nearly twice the dead, in the attacks that dominate the news and shape how Americans feel about public life.

The United States has tested this policy. The 1994 federal assault weapons ban barred the manufacture and sale of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, and it grandfathered existing stock rather than confiscating it. It expired on September 13, 2004. Federal assessments found the use of banned guns in crime declined in the cities studied, while concluding that with grandfathered stock still circulating, the ban's effect on overall violence remained uncertain; newer research finds that restrictions on large-capacity magazines are associated with fewer deaths in high-fatality mass shootings. A modern ban should apply to future manufacture and sale, and this time pair it with a buyback that shrinks the grandfathered stock.

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require an NICS check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales arranged at gun shows and online, so that the standard a licensed dealer must meet applies to every sale.
2. **Reinstate and strengthen the assault weapons ban.** Restore the 1994 ban's prohibition on the manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, fund a voluntary buyback to reduce the grandfathered stock, and write definitions by function so the industry cannot engineer around them.
3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Appropriate dedicated, multiyear funding for firearm injury prevention research at a scale commensurate with a toll of 46,728 deaths, and codify that federal research on the causes and prevention of gun violence is authorized public health work.
4. **Help states adopt extreme-risk laws.** Create a competitive grant program for states that enact extreme-risk protection orders, which allow courts to temporarily separate firearms from people who pose a documented danger to themselves or others, and condition funds on strong due-process protections. Indiana's decade of experience with a risk-based seizure law is associated with a 7.5 percent drop in firearm suicides.

## Closing the gaps

None of these numbers describes an act of nature. They describe the predictable results of laws that stop halfway: checks that apply to some sellers and not others, and a rifle ban that was allowed to expire with its stock grandfathered in place. Congress wrote those gaps into law, and Congress can write them out. The families behind this year's figures should not have to accept them.

# Data appendix: Safer Communities Brief No. 9

"Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban"
Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention, Northgate Progress Institute
Publication date: Tuesday, October 27, 2026

| Indicator | 2023 |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths | 46,728 |
| Equivalent frequency | one death every 11 minutes |
| Rank among all years on record | third-highest annual total |
| Change in overall gun death rate from 2022 | down about 3 percent |
| Composition (for reference; see B3 note) | suicides 27,300 (58%); homicides 17,927 |

Note: The total spans all intents. JHU reports that gun suicides were 58 percent of the 2023 total, a record high, and that gun homicides declined for a second straight year. One death every 11 minutes is 525,600 minutes divided by 46,728 deaths.

## Table 2. Children and teens ages 1-17, 2023

| Indicator | Value |
|---|---|
| Deaths | 2,566 |
| Rate | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Deaths per day | about 7 |
| Leading cause of death | firearms, 4th consecutive year, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses |
| Intent: homicide | 63% |
| Intent: suicide | 29% |
| Intent: unintentional | 5% |
| Intent: undetermined or other | 3% |

Source: CDC WONDER, 2023 final data, tabulated in Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, "Gun Violence in the United States 2023," June 2025.

Note: JHU reports the ages 1-17 death rate rose about 2 percent from 2022. House phrasing per style sheet B2: deaths of children and teens are described as "children shot and killed."

## Table 3. Youth firearm death rate, ages 1-19

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Rate, ages 1-19, pooled 2021-2023 | 5.9 per 100,000 |

Source: America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, "Firearm deaths among children ages 1-19," pooled 2021-2023, from CDC WONDER.

Note for editors: this is the series rate carried in style sheet B2. It is not a single-year children's rate: it includes 18- and 19-year-olds, who are legal adults with markedly higher gun death rates, and it pools three years, including the 2021 record year. The 2023 single-year rate for ages 1-17 is 3.7 per 100,000 (Table 2). Brief No. 9 uses the ages 1-17 figure and cites this measure only with its full label. Sign-off required if the campaign wants it used unlabeled.

## Table 4. Firearm acquisitions without a background check

| Estimate | Figure | What was measured |
|---|---|---|
| 2015 national survey | 22% | of gun owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years, those who acquired it without a background check |
| 1994 NSPOF, original estimate | about 40% | of recently acquired guns came from a source other than a licensed dealer, including gifts and inheritances |
| 1994 NSPOF, sales-only reanalysis | 14-22% | share of sales, not acquisitions, without a background check |

Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, "Firearm acquisition without background checks: results of a national survey," Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017 (2015 survey, n=1,613 gun owners); Cook and Ludwig, "Guns in America: National Survey on Private Ownership and Use of Firearms," National Institute of Justice, 1997 (1994 NSPOF survey). Series source line per style sheet B6: "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research."

Note for editors: the 1994 NSPOF did not ask about background checks and predates full implementation of the Brady Act; the "40 percent of gun sales" formulation has been rated Mostly False (PolitiFact, February 2018) and called stale (Washington Post Fact Checker, January 2013). Brief No. 9 therefore leads with the direct 2015 figure (22 percent) and does not use the B1 series line as written. Sign-off required.

## Table 5. Public support for background checks on all gun buyers

| Poll | Population | Support |
|---|---|---|
| Quinnipiac University national poll, November 2023 | registered voters | 92% |

Source: Quinnipiac University Polling Institute, national survey of registered voters, November 2, 2023.

Note: separate national surveying of gun owners (97Percent, December 2024, n=5,100 gun owners who are registered voters) finds about 85 percent support universal background checks.

## Table 6. Research evidence on background-check laws

| Policy | Evidence finding |
|---|---|
| Dealer background checks | moderate evidence of a reduction in firearm homicide |
| Universal background checks (dealer plus private sales) | moderate evidence of a reduction in total homicide; limited evidence on firearm homicide |
| Universal background checks and suicide | inconclusive |

Source: RAND, Gun Policy in America, "The Effects of Background Checks" evidence review (accessed October 2026); RAND, "The Science of Gun Policy" (fifth edition; accessed October 2026).

Note: RAND grades studies it considers methodologically adequate; "inconclusive" means the available studies do not yet support a conclusion, not that evidence of no effect was found.

## Table 7. Mass shootings, 2023

Source: Gun Violence Archive, "Mass Shootings" report, 2023; killed and injured counts as compiled by Axios, January 9, 2024; AP/USA Today/Northeastern University mass-killing database, October 2023.

Note: GVA defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter; the AP/USA Today/Northeastern database counts four or more killed. The two counts answer different questions and are not comparable. GVA is a private nonprofit data project, not a federal dataset; the series source line "Federal data (CDC, FBI) and peer-reviewed research" does not cover this table. Per style sheet B4 the series framing is "mass shootings like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston"; those attacks (2022, 2018, 2023) were carried out with AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles.

## Table 8. Rifles in U.S. murders (all rifle types)

| Year | Share of murders | Count |
|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 2.6% of murders | count not carried in the source table |
| 2018 | 2.8% | 297 murders |

Source: FBI, Uniform Crime Reports Expanded Homicide Data, 2017 and 2018.

Note: the FBI does not separate AR-style rifles from other rifles. The brief's assault weapons argument rests on lethality in public mass shootings (Table 9), not on rifles' overall share of murders, which is under 3 percent.

## Table 9. Lethality of active shooter incidents with and without semiautomatic rifles

| Measure | With semiautomatic rifle | Without |
|---|---|---|
| Share of incidents, 2000-2017 | 24.6% (61 of 248) | 75.4% (187) |
| Mean persons wounded | 5.48 | 3.02 |
| Mean persons killed | 4.25 | 2.49 |
| Mean persons wounded or killed | 9.72 | 5.47 |
| Incidence rate ratio, wounded | 1.81 (95% CI, 1.30-2.53) | |
| Incidence rate ratio, killed | 1.97 (95% CI, 1.38-2.80) | |

Source: de Jager, Goralnick, McCarty, Hashmi, Jarman and Haider, "Lethality of civilian active shooter incidents with and without semiautomatic rifles in the United States," JAMA, 2018.

Note: the share of wounded people who died was similar in both groups (about 44 percent with a semiautomatic rifle present); the difference in deaths is driven by more people being shot, not by deadlier wounds. Handguns remain the most common firearm in mass shootings (used in about 80 percent of attacks per The Violence Project database), so the series line "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings" (style sheet B5) is not supported as written. The defensible series line is that assault weapons are the weapon of choice in the deadliest mass shootings. Sign-off required.

## Table 10. Federal assault weapons ban, 1994-2004

| Provision or finding | Detail |
|---|---|
| Enacted | September 1994 |
| Prohibited | manufacture and sale of new semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines (more than 10 rounds) |
| Existing stock | grandfathered; no confiscation |
| Expiration | September 13, 2004 |
| NIJ assessment of banned-gun use in crime | declined 17% to 72% across the localities studied (1995-2003 post-ban period) |
| NIJ assessment of overall crime effect | uncertain; grandfathered stock limited measurable effect |
| RAND evidence grade for bans' effect on violent crime and mass shootings | inconclusive |
| Large-capacity magazine bans and high-fatality mass shootings | associated with fewer deaths |

Source: Koper, "Updated Assessment of the Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Impacts on Gun Markets and Gun Violence, 1994-2003," National Institute of Justice, 2004; RAND, "The Science of Gun Policy" (fifth edition; accessed October 2026); Klarevas, McCartney and Vernick, "Assessing the potential to reduce deaths and injuries from mass shootings through restrictions on assault weapons and other high-capacity semiautomatic firearms," Criminology and Public Policy, 2019.

Note: the same research review finds high-capacity semiautomatics (assault weapons as a subset) used in 20 to 58 percent of firearm mass murders, and in a particularly high share of public mass shootings. Recommendation 2's buyback proposal is designed to address the grandfathering constraint NIJ identified.

## Table 11. Extreme-risk (red flag) laws: suicide outcomes

| State | Finding |
|---|---|
| Indiana | risk-based firearm seizure law (2006) associated with a 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides over 10 years |
| Connecticut | law (1999) associated with a 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides in the post-Virginia Tech enforcement period |

Source: Kivisto and Phalen, "Effects of risk-based firearm seizure laws in Connecticut and Indiana on suicide rates, 1981-2015," Psychiatric Services, 2018.

Note: RAND grades the broader ERPO literature as inconclusive for suicide overall; the Connecticut and Indiana studies are the strongest quasi-experimental evidence and used synthetic controls. Recommendation 4 includes due-process conditions in part to answer the objections raised in this literature.

## Definitions

- **Assault weapons:** semiautomatic firearms with detachable magazines and the military-style features defined in the 1994 federal ban (style sheet A2). The outline's category is the one used in Table 10.
- **Mass shooting:** four or more people shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter (Gun Violence Archive).
- **Universal background checks:** extension of the licensed-dealer NICS requirement to all firearm sales and transfers.

## Series figures used from the fall campaign (style sheet B1-B5), with handling

| Series figure | Handling in this package |
|---|---|
| B1: "40% of gun sales take place without a background check" | not used as written; replaced with 22% (2015 survey) and the 14-22% sales reanalysis; provenance in Table 4 |
| B2: ages 1-19 rate (5.9 per 100,000) as the rate for "children" | used only with its full label; brief leads with ages 1-17 (3.7 per 100,000); see Table 3 note |
| B3: 46,728 "killed by gun violence," no intent breakdown | used in all persuasive copy per B3; composition rows retained in appendix Table 1 |
| B4: 656 mass shootings (GVA), "like Uvalde, Parkland and Lewiston" | used; definitional note in Table 7 |
| B5: "assault weapons are the weapon of choice in America's mass shootings" | not used as written; replaced with the lethality finding (Table 9) and "deadliest mass shootings" framing; see Table 9 note |

# Fact sheet: Closing the gaps on gun violence

**Safer Communities Brief No. 9** | Northgate Progress Institute | October 27, 2026
For use by congressional offices. Full citations and notes: data appendix to Brief No. 9.

## Eight numbers for the record

**1. 46,728** Americans killed by gun violence in 2023. One every 11 minutes; the third-highest annual total on record, down about 3 percent from 2022.
Source: CDC WONDER 2023 final data, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**2. 2,566** children and teens ages 1-17 killed by gun violence in 2023: 3.7 per 100,000, about seven young people every day.
Source: CDC WONDER 2023 final data, via Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025.

**3. Fourth straight year** firearms were the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1-17, ahead of car crashes, cancer and drug overdoses.
Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, analysis of CDC WONDER 2023 data, June 2025.

**4. 22 percent** of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years acquired it without a background check (2015 national survey of 1,613 owners).
Source: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017.

**5. 92 percent** of registered voters support requiring background checks for all gun buyers.
Source: Quinnipiac University national poll, November 2023.

**6. 656** mass shootings in 2023, four or more people shot per incident, excluding the shooter: 712 killed and 2,692 injured.
Source: Gun Violence Archive, 2023; casualty compilation by Axios, January 2024.

**7. About twice as many killed and wounded** in active shooter attacks when a semiautomatic rifle is present (mean 4.25 killed and 5.48 wounded per incident, versus 2.49 and 3.02 without).
Source: de Jager et al., JAMA, 2018.

**8. 7.5 percent fewer** firearm suicides in Indiana over a decade following its risk-based firearm seizure law.
Source: Kivisto and Phalen, Psychiatric Services, 2018.

## What Brief No. 9 asks Congress to do

1. Pass universal background checks, covering private sales at gun shows and online.
2. Reinstate the assault weapons ban, bar large-capacity magazines, and fund a voluntary buyback of grandfathered stock.
3. Fund firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and NIH at a scale commensurate with a toll of 46,728 deaths.
4. Create a matching grant program, with due-process conditions, for states that enact extreme-risk protection orders.

Media contact: Northgate Progress Institute Office of Communications, Washington, DC.

# Press release: Safer Communities Brief No. 9

**EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE UNTIL TUESDAY, OCTOBER 27, 2026, 10:00 A.M. ET**
Do not publish or post before that time.

Media contact: [NPI communications office to confirm name, phone and email]

## Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban would save lives, NPI brief finds

WASHINGTON, October 27, 2026. Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and firearms remained the leading cause of death for children and teens ages 1 to 17 for the fourth straight year, according to a brief released today by the Northgate Progress Institute.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Senior Fellow Dr. Jamal Whitfield, argues that two gaps in federal law cost lives: a background-check requirement that exempts private sales, and the 2004 expiration of the assault weapons ban.

The brief finds 22 percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the prior two years got no background check, while 92 percent of registered voters support checks on all gun buyers. It documents 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 dead and 2,692 injured, and finds attacks with semiautomatic rifles kill and wound about twice as many people.

"Every figure in this brief is a family's grief," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention at NPI. "The gaps that let guns reach dangerous hands, and put battlefield rifles on our main streets, were written into federal law. They were choices, and Congress can make different ones."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks covering private sales; reinstate the assault weapons ban with new restrictions on large-capacity magazines and a voluntary buyback of grandfathered stock; fund firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and NIH; and help states enact extreme-risk laws with due-process protections.

The brief, fact sheet and data appendix are available from the institute. The Northgate Progress Institute is a Washington, DC think tank working to expand economic security, protect public health and make communities safer.
